Yes, you're right, and it's not pedantry: the two quantities answer different questions, and the gap is large in practice.

A p-value of 0.03 is P(data at least this extreme | null true). The "97% chance the hypothesis is true" claim is P(hypothesis | data), which also requires a prior and the alternative's plausibility. Even the reading "97% chance the null is false" doesn't follow.

How far apart they can be: under the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound, p = 0.03 corresponds to a Bayes factor of at best about 0.29 against the null. With a 50/50 prior, that leaves the null at roughly 22% or more, not 3%. With a skeptical prior (say 10% of tested hypotheses are true), the null stays more likely than not. That is the mechanism behind many failed replications.

The inference being wrong in practice, not just in wording, is the point to make to your colleague.
